## A number hiding inside a magnet

Take an ordinary refrigerator magnet and warm it gently with a hairdryer. Nothing dramatic happens. Heat it in a furnace, though, and something remarkable occurs: at a precise temperature the magnet abruptly *forgets* it was ever a magnet. Its grip on the fridge vanishes, not gradually but at a sharp threshold. Cool it back down and, at the very same temperature, magnetism springs back to life out of nowhere.

That threshold is called the **Curie temperature**, and the sudden change of character around it is a **phase transition** — the same kind of qualitative jump that turns ice into water or water into steam. For more than a century physicists have asked a deceptively simple question: starting from the microscopic rules that govern how individual atoms tug on their neighbors, can we *predict* exactly where that threshold sits?

For one idealized but profoundly important model of a magnet — the two-dimensional **Ising model** — the answer is yes, and it is breathtakingly clean. The critical point is governed by a single transcendental equation,

$$\sinh(2\beta) = 1,$$

whose solution is the elegant constant

$$\beta_c = \tfrac{1}{2}\log\!\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right) \approx 0.4407,$$

and correspondingly the critical temperature

$$T_c = \frac{2}{\log\!\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right)} \approx 2.2692$$

(in natural units where the coupling strength and Boltzmann's constant are set to one). This article tells the story of where that number comes from, why the golden-ratio-flavored $1+\sqrt{2}$ appears, and what a deep symmetry called *duality* reveals about it.

## A grid of tiny arrows

The Ising model strips magnetism down to its barest cartoon. Imagine an enormous checkerboard. On every square sits a tiny arrow — a **spin** — that can point only one of two ways: up ($+1$) or down ($-1$). That's it. No continuous angles, no quantum subtleties at first glance, just a sea of binary switches.

The physics lives in a single rule: **neighbors prefer to agree**. Two adjacent spins pointing the same way are happy and contribute low energy; two pointing opposite ways are frustrated and cost energy. If we write $\sigma_i = \pm 1$ for the spin at site $i$, the total energy of a configuration is

$$E = -\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} \sigma_i \sigma_j,$$

where the sum runs over all neighboring pairs $\langle i, j\rangle$. Aligned neighbors lower the energy; misaligned neighbors raise it.

Now bring in temperature. Nature does not simply minimize energy; it balances energy against *disorder*. The probability of seeing a particular configuration $\sigma$ is given by the **Boltzmann weight**

$$P(\sigma) \propto e^{-\beta E(\sigma)},$$

where $\beta = 1/T$ is the **inverse temperature**. When $\beta$ is large (cold), low-energy ordered states dominate and the spins want to line up. When $\beta$ is small (hot), thermal agitation wins and the spins point every which way, washing out any net magnetism.

Between these two regimes lies the drama. Somewhere there must be a tipping point — a special $\beta_c$ — separating the ordered, magnetized world from the disordered, demagnetized one. The whole game is to find it.

## The miracle of two dimensions

In one dimension — a single chain of spins — there is no drama at all. A famous calculation shows that a 1D Ising chain never spontaneously magnetizes at any positive temperature: a single break in the chain costs only a fixed amount of energy but can sit in enormously many places, so disorder always wins. The chain has no phase transition.

In two dimensions everything changes, and the reason is geometric. To separate a region of "up" spins from a sea of "down" spins on a 2D grid, you must draw a *closed loop* — a domain wall — around it. Long walls cost a lot of energy, and crucially, the number of long walls does not grow fast enough to overwhelm that cost when the temperature is low enough. Order can survive. This intuition, due to Rudolf Peierls, is the **Peierls argument**, and it proves that the 2D model genuinely does have an ordered low-temperature phase — there really is a nontrivial threshold to find.

Finding the *exact* location of that threshold was a tour de force. Lars Onsager achieved it in 1944 in one of the legendary calculations of theoretical physics, deriving the full thermodynamics of the 2D model in closed form. But there is a shortcut to the *location* of the transition — not its full behavior, but the precise number $\beta_c$ — that requires far less heavy machinery and exposes a gorgeous hidden symmetry. That shortcut is **Kramers–Wannier duality**.

## A mirror between hot and cold

Hendrik Kramers and Gregory Wannier discovered, in 1941, that the 2D Ising model contains a secret mirror. There is a transformation that takes the model at one temperature and turns it into the *same kind of model* at a different temperature — but with hot and cold swapped. A very cold, highly ordered system gets reflected into a very hot, highly disordered one, and vice versa.

The dictionary connecting a temperature $\beta$ to its mirror image $\beta^*$ is the elegant relation

$$\sinh(2\beta)\,\sinh(2\beta^*) = 1.$$

Read it carefully. If $\beta$ is large, then $\sinh(2\beta)$ is large, so $\sinh(2\beta^*)$ must be small, forcing $\beta^*$ to be small. High temperature maps to low temperature; the mirror flips the thermometer.

Here is the punchline. The system can have *only one* phase transition (this is a known fact about the model). The duality maps the high-temperature disordered phase to the low-temperature ordered phase. So the single critical point cannot live anywhere except the one place the mirror leaves untouched — the **self-dual point**, where $\beta$ equals its own reflection, $\beta = \beta^*$. Plug that into the duality dictionary and the two factors merge into one:

$$\sinh(2\beta_c)^2 = 1, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \sinh(2\beta_c) = 1.$$

The entire problem of locating the phase transition collapses into solving a single, clean equation. No infinite sums, no transfer-matrix eigenvalues — just $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$.

## Solving the equation, and why $1+\sqrt{2}$ appears

Solving $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$ is a pleasant piece of algebra. Recall that

$$\sinh(x) = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}.$$

Set $x = 2\beta$ and let $u = e^x$. The equation $\sinh(x) = 1$ becomes

$$\frac{u - u^{-1}}{2} = 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; u^2 - 2u - 1 = 0.$$

The quadratic formula gives $u = 1 \pm \sqrt{2}$, and since $u = e^{2\beta}$ must be positive we take

$$e^{2\beta_c} = 1 + \sqrt{2}.$$

Taking logarithms yields the headline constant,

$$\beta_c = \tfrac{1}{2}\log\!\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right),$$

and inverting to get the temperature $T_c = 1/\beta_c$ gives

$$T_c = \frac{2}{\log\!\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right)} \approx 2.2692.$$

The mysterious "silver ratio" $1 + \sqrt{2}$ is no coincidence: it is exactly the positive root of $u^2 = 2u + 1$, which is precisely what $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$ demands. The geometry of the square lattice, refracted through the duality mirror, distills into this one quadratic.

It is worth pausing on a beautiful self-consistency check. The constant $\beta_c$ has a remarkable companion identity:

$$(1 + \sqrt{2})^{-1} = \sqrt{2} - 1.$$

You can verify it directly — multiply $(1+\sqrt 2)(\sqrt 2 - 1) = \sqrt 2 - 1 + 2 - \sqrt 2 = 1$. This tiny fact is exactly the algebraic engine that makes the duality work: the reciprocal that appears when you reflect a temperature is itself a clean number of the same family, and it is what guarantees that evaluating $\sinh$ at $\log(1+\sqrt 2)$ lands precisely on $1$.

## Why this is the *only* answer

A skeptic might worry: maybe $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$ has several solutions, and we picked the wrong one. It does not. The function $\sinh$ is *strictly increasing* across the entire real line — every output value is hit exactly once. So the equation $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$ has a single solution, full stop, and we have found it. The self-dual point is unique.

We can package the logic even more tightly. For a genuine (positive) inverse temperature $\beta > 0$, the self-duality fixed-point condition

$$\sinh(2\beta)^2 = 1$$

holds **if and only if** $\beta = \beta_c$. The "if" direction is the substitution we just did. The "only if" direction uses two facts: for positive $\beta$ the quantity $\sinh(2\beta)$ is itself positive, so squaring-to-one forces $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$ (the other root, $-1$, is excluded); and then strict monotonicity pins down $\beta$ uniquely. This crisp equivalence is the mathematical heart of the whole story: the critical point is *characterized*, not merely computed.

## What the number means in the lab

The abstract checkerboard is not just a toy. The 2D Ising model is the prototype for an astonishing range of real phenomena that share the same mathematical skeleton:

- **Magnetism.** Thin magnetic films and layered materials behave, near their ordering temperatures, almost exactly like the 2D Ising model. The very concept of a sharp Curie point is what the model explains.
- **Liquid–vapor and binary alloys.** Replace "spin up/down" with "atom present/absent" or "atom type A/type B," and the same energy bookkeeping describes how fluids condense and how metal alloys separate into domains. The Ising critical point and the liquid–gas critical point are, mathematically, the *same* critical point.
- **Universality.** Perhaps the deepest lesson is that wildly different physical systems — a magnet, a fluid, an alloy — display *identical* behavior near their critical points. They fall into the same "universality class." The 2D Ising model is the cornerstone example, and its exactly known critical point is the calibration standard against which simulations and experiments are checked.

When a physicist runs a Monte Carlo simulation of a 2D magnet and watches the magnetization collapse, the temperature at which it collapses had better be $T_c \approx 2.2692$. That number, born from $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$, is the benchmark the entire field trusts.

## The shape of the argument

Step back and admire the architecture. We began with a microscopic rule so simple a child could play it — arrows on a grid that like to agree. We added temperature as a tug-of-war between order and chaos. We noted, via the Peierls loop-counting argument, that in two dimensions order can genuinely survive at low temperature, so a real transition must exist. Then a hidden symmetry — the Kramers–Wannier mirror swapping hot and cold — forced the lone transition to sit exactly at the point fixed by the mirror. That fixed-point condition was a single equation, $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$, and a line of algebra turned it into the silver ratio $1 + \sqrt{2}$ and the constant $\beta_c = \tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt 2)$.

Three short statements capture the whole edifice:

1. **The critical value.** $\sinh(2\beta_c) = 1$, where $\beta_c = \tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$ — the self-dual point really does satisfy the equation.
2. **Uniqueness.** Any positive $\beta$ with $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$ must equal $\beta_c$ — there is no other candidate.
3. **The duality characterization.** For $\beta > 0$, the fixed-point condition $\sinh(2\beta)^2 = 1$ holds exactly when $\beta = \beta_c$ — critical and self-dual are one and the same.

There is also a satisfying consistency relation between the two ways of naming the threshold, by temperature and by inverse temperature: $T_c \cdot \beta_c = 1$, exactly as it must be, since one is the reciprocal of the other.

## A thread from Onsager to the present

Onsager's 1944 solution remains a monument of mathematical physics, and the Kramers–Wannier duality that preceded it has grown into a vast subject — dualities now organize our understanding of everything from gauge theories to quantum field theory to the modern study of topological phases of matter. The little equation $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$ is a doorway. Behind it lie infinite-volume limits, contour expansions, the exact spontaneous magnetization curve, and the rich machinery of conformal field theory that describes the critical point's fractal-scale behavior.

But the doorway itself is something to savor. A magnet's most dramatic act — waking up, all at once, at a sharp temperature — is governed by a number you can derive in an afternoon from a single hyperbolic equation, with a silver ratio glinting at its core. That a phenomenon so vivid in the physical world should resolve into algebra so clean is one of the quiet miracles that keeps mathematicians and physicists coming back to the humble grid of tiny arrows.

$$\beta_c = \tfrac{1}{2}\log\!\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right) \approx 0.4406868,$$

We additionally record the reciprocity $T_c \cdot \beta_c = 1$ and the positivity $\beta_c > 0$. The arguments rest only on elementary properties of the hyperbolic sine — its analytic form, strict monotonicity, and sign on the positive axis — illustrating how the deep statistical-mechanical content of the duality is, at the level of the critical point, captured by a single transcendental equation. We frame the result physically (Boltzmann weights, the Peierls argument for the existence of a transition, and the duality map relating high and low temperature), give complete proof sketches, present numerical demonstrations, and outline a program for formalizing the full duality and finite-volume partition function.

## 1. Introduction

The Ising model is the canonical lattice model of cooperative phenomena. Introduced by Wilhelm Lenz and studied in one dimension by Ernst Ising, it assigns to each site of a lattice a binary spin $\sigma_i \in \{-1, +1\}$ and weights configurations by an energy that rewards aligned neighbors. Despite its simplicity it captures the essence of a ferromagnetic phase transition and serves as the prototype for the modern theory of critical phenomena and universality.

In two dimensions on the square lattice, the model is exactly solvable. Lars Onsager's 1944 solution computed the free energy in closed form and revealed a logarithmic divergence of the specific heat at a sharp critical temperature. The *location* of that temperature, however, can be pinned down by a more elementary and structurally illuminating route: the duality discovered by Kramers and Wannier in 1941, which relates the model at inverse temperature $\beta$ to the model at a *dual* inverse temperature $\beta^*$ with hot and cold interchanged. Granting that the model has a single transition, that transition must occur at the unique *self-dual* point, and the self-duality condition reduces to the transcendental equation

$$\sinh(2\beta) = 1. \tag{$\star$}$$

This paper provides a rigorous, self-contained treatment of the constant defined by $(\star)$. We isolate the purely analytic core of the argument — that $(\star)$ has a unique solution, given in closed form by $\beta_c = \tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$ — and prove it, along with the natural variants involving the squared duality condition and the critical temperature. We are deliberate about which facts are statistical-mechanical inputs (the existence and uniqueness of the phase transition, and the form of the duality relation) and which are theorems we prove here (the solution and characterization of $(\star)$).

### 1.1 Notation and conventions

We work over the real numbers $\mathbb{R}$. The hyperbolic sine is

$$\sinh(x) = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2},$$

with the standard logarithm $\log$ and principal square root $\sqrt{\cdot}$. We adopt natural units in which the nearest-neighbor coupling $J$ and Boltzmann constant $k_B$ are set to $1$, so that $\beta = 1/T$. All "temperatures" are dimensionless.

## 2. Physical setting

### 2.1 The model

Let $\Lambda$ be a finite subset of the square lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$ (for definiteness, an $m \times n$ torus). A *configuration* is a map $\sigma : \Lambda \to \{-1, +1\}$. The (ferromagnetic, zero-field) **Hamiltonian** is

$$H(\sigma) = -\sum_{\langle i, j\rangle} \sigma_i \sigma_j,$$

where $\langle i, j \rangle$ ranges over nearest-neighbor pairs. Aligned pairs contribute $-1$ (favorable), anti-aligned pairs contribute $+1$.

The **Gibbs (Boltzmann) measure** at inverse temperature $\beta > 0$ assigns to each configuration the probability

$$P_\beta(\sigma) = \frac{1}{Z(\beta)}\, e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}, \qquad Z(\beta) = \sum_{\sigma} e^{-\beta H(\sigma)},$$

with $Z(\beta)$ the **partition function**. The order parameter is the magnetization $m(\beta) = \lim_{\Lambda \uparrow \mathbb{Z}^2} \langle \sigma_0 \rangle_\beta$ (with $+$ boundary conditions); it is positive in the ordered phase and zero in the disordered phase.

### 2.2 Existence of a transition: the Peierls argument

That the 2D model has a genuinely ordered phase at large $\beta$ is the content of the Peierls argument. A configuration deviating from the all-$+$ ground state is organized into **contours**: closed domain walls on the dual lattice separating $+$ and $-$ regions. A contour of length $L$ is suppressed by a Boltzmann factor $e^{-2\beta L}$, while the number of contours of length $L$ surrounding a fixed site grows only like $C^L$ for a fixed constant $C$. For $\beta$ large enough that $e^{-2\beta} C < 1$, the summed probability that a given site is encircled by some contour is strictly less than $\tfrac12$, so $\langle \sigma_0 \rangle_\beta > 0$: spontaneous magnetization survives. This establishes the *existence* of a low-temperature ordered phase, hence of a critical $\beta_c$ separating it from the high-temperature disordered phase. (By contrast, in one dimension the analogous contours are point defects whose entropy always defeats their energy cost, and no transition occurs.)

### 2.3 Kramers–Wannier duality and the self-dual point

The high-temperature expansion of $Z(\beta)$ organizes the partition function as a sum over *even subgraphs* (closed loops) of $\Lambda$, weighted by powers of $\tanh\beta$. The low-temperature expansion organizes it as a sum over *contours* on the dual lattice, weighted by powers of $e^{-2\beta}$. On the square lattice these two expansions have the same combinatorial structure, and matching them yields the **duality relation** between $\beta$ and a dual inverse temperature $\beta^*$,

$$\sinh(2\beta)\,\sinh(2\beta^*) = 1, \tag{KW}$$

under which $Z(\beta)$ and $Z(\beta^*)$ are proportional up to an explicit smooth prefactor. The map $\beta \mapsto \beta^*$ is a strictly order-reversing involution of $(0,\infty)$: large $\beta$ (cold, ordered) corresponds to small $\beta^*$ (hot, disordered).

Because the smooth prefactor cannot create a singularity, any non-analyticity of the free energy at $\beta$ must be mirrored at $\beta^*$. If the model has exactly one transition, it cannot be split between two distinct dual temperatures; it must sit at the unique **self-dual** point $\beta = \beta^*$. Setting $\beta^* = \beta$ in (KW) gives

$$\sinh(2\beta)^2 = 1, \qquad\text{i.e. for } \beta > 0,\quad \sinh(2\beta) = 1, \tag{$\star$}$$

the equation whose solution is the subject of this paper.

> **Scope.** The existence of a single transition and the derivation of (KW) are statistical-mechanical inputs (sketched above and listed as future formalization targets in §8). The contribution formalized here is the rigorous solution and characterization of the self-dual equation $(\star)$ and the closed form of the resulting constant.

We fix the two protagonists.

**Definition 3.1 (Critical inverse temperature).**

**Definition 3.2 (Critical temperature).**
$$T_c := \frac{2}{\log\!\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right)}.$$

Numerically, $\log(1+\sqrt2) = \log(2.41421356\ldots) = 0.88137358\ldots$, so $\beta_c = 0.44068679\ldots$ and $T_c = 2.26918531\ldots$.

**Lemma 4.1 (Reciprocal identity).**
$$(1 + \sqrt{2})^{-1} = \sqrt{2} - 1.$$

*Sketch.* Since $\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2 = 2$, we have $(\sqrt2 - 1)(1 + \sqrt2) = \sqrt2 + 2 - 1 - \sqrt2 = 1$. Hence $\sqrt2 - 1$ is the multiplicative inverse of $1 + \sqrt2$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Theorem 4.2 (Critical value: the self-dual point solves $(\star)$).**
$$\sinh(2\beta_c) = 1.$$

We claim $(\sqrt2 - 1)(1 + \sqrt2) = 1$. Expanding,

using $\sqrt2 \cdot \sqrt2 = 2$. A real number with a left inverse in a field is invertible with that inverse, so $(1 + \sqrt2)^{-1} = \sqrt2 - 1$. $\blacksquare$

### 5.2 The critical value (Theorem 4.2)

$$\sinh(\log x) = \frac{e^{\log x} - e^{-\log x}}{2} = \frac{x - x^{-1}}{2}.$$
By Lemma 4.1, $x^{-1} = \sqrt2 - 1$, hence
$$\sinh(2\beta_c) = \frac{(1+\sqrt2) - (\sqrt2 - 1)}{2} = \frac{2}{2} = 1. \qquad \blacksquare$$

### 5.3 Uniqueness (Theorem 4.3)

The derivative of $\sinh$ is $\cosh$, and $\cosh(x) \geq 1$ for all $x$, so $\sinh$ is strictly increasing and therefore injective on $\mathbb{R}$. Because $\sqrt2 > 0$ we have $1 + \sqrt2 > 1$; the logarithm is strictly increasing with $\log 1 = 0$, so $\log(1+\sqrt2) > 0$, and $\beta_c = \tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2) > 0$. For reciprocity, set $L = \log(1+\sqrt2) \neq 0$; then $T_c\,\beta_c = (2/L)(L/2) = 1$. $\blacksquare$

### 5.5 Fixed-point characterization (Theorem 4.6)

($\Leftarrow$) Immediate from Theorem 4.2 by squaring. ($\Rightarrow$) Assume $\beta > 0$ and $\sinh(2\beta)^2 = 1$. Since $2\beta > 0$ and $\sinh$ is positive on the positive axis, $s := \sinh(2\beta) > 0$. From $s^2 = 1$ and $s > 0$ we conclude $s = 1$. Theorem 4.3 then gives $\beta = \beta_c$. $\blacksquare$

---

## 6. Algorithms

The constant $\beta_c$ and the surrounding structure are eminently computable. We record three algorithms used in the demonstrations of §7.

### 6.1 Closed-form evaluation of $\beta_c$ and $T_c$

The most direct computation evaluates the closed forms of Definitions 3.1–3.2 in floating point and verifies the defining identity $\sinh(2\beta_c) = 1$ to machine precision. Complexity is $O(1)$.

### 6.2 Root-finding cross-check via bisection

To corroborate the closed form *without* using it, one can solve $(\star)$ numerically. The function $f(\beta) = \sinh(2\beta) - 1$ is continuous and strictly increasing, with $f(0) = -1 < 0$ and $f(1) = \sinh(2) - 1 > 0$, so a unique root lies in $(0,1)$. Bisection converges linearly, halving the bracket each step; $n$ steps yield an absolute error below $2^{-n}$. The recovered root agrees with $\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$.

### 6.3 Duality involution and its fixed point

Given the relation (KW), the dual map is $\beta^*(\beta) = \tfrac12\,\operatorname{arcsinh}\!\big(1/\sinh(2\beta)\big)$. Iterating or directly solving $\beta^*(\beta) = \beta$ recovers the self-dual point. Verifying that $\beta^*(\beta^*(\beta)) = \beta$ (involutivity) and that $\beta^*(\beta_c) = \beta_c$ (the fixed point) provides an independent structural check.

---

## 7. Numerical demonstrations

The accompanying `demo.py` performs the following, all to high precision:

1. **Closed-form values.** Computes $\beta_c = 0.4406867935\ldots$ and $T_c = 2.2691853142\ldots$ and confirms $\beta_c = 1/T_c$ (Theorem 4.5).
2. **The defining identity.** Evaluates $\sinh(2\beta_c)$ and finds $1$ to within machine epsilon (Theorem 4.2), and $\sinh(2\beta_c)^2 = 1$ (Theorem 4.6).
3. **Reciprocal identity.** Verifies $(1+\sqrt2)^{-1} = \sqrt2 - 1$ numerically (Lemma 4.1).
4. **Uniqueness by bisection.** Solves $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$ on $(0,1)$ by bisection and matches the closed form (Theorems 4.3, 6.2).
5. **Duality involution.** Confirms $\beta^* \circ \beta^* = \mathrm{id}$ on samples and that $\beta_c$ is the unique fixed point (§6.3).
6. **Monotone uniqueness.** Tabulates $\sinh(2\beta)$ to exhibit strict monotonicity, illustrating why the solution is unique.

---

## 8. Applications and significance

**Universality and benchmarking.** The 2D Ising critical point is the reference standard for the study of critical phenomena. Its exact value calibrates Monte Carlo simulations, finite-size scaling analyses, and series-expansion estimates; any numerical method for the model is validated against $T_c = 2.2691853\ldots$.

**Mapping to other systems.** Through the lattice-gas correspondence ($\sigma_i = 2n_i - 1$ with occupation $n_i \in \{0,1\}$), the Ising transition is the same critical point as the liquid–vapor transition and as phase separation in binary alloys. The single constant governs the onset of order in this entire universality class.

**Dualities as a paradigm.** Kramers–Wannier duality is the historical seed of a vast modern subject. Order/disorder duality, the recognition that a self-dual point pins a transition, and the general philosophy of relating a theory at strong coupling to a (possibly different) theory at weak coupling all trace to this example. The self-dual equation $(\star)$ is the simplest nontrivial instance of "the critical point is the fixed point of a duality."

---

## 9. Discussion

The treatment here deliberately separates two layers. The *physical* layer — existence and uniqueness of the transition (Peierls) and the duality relation (KW) — supplies the reason the critical point coincides with the self-dual point. The *analytic* layer — solving $(\star)$ — is what we have made fully rigorous: the closed form $\beta_c = \tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$, its uniqueness via strict monotonicity of $\sinh$, the positivity of $\sinh$ on $(0,\infty)$ that promotes $\sinh^2 = 1$ to $\sinh = 1$, and the reciprocity $T_c \beta_c = 1$. A pleasant feature is how little machinery the analytic layer requires: the entire qualitative picture of the duality (it swaps hot and cold and has a single self-dual point) is encoded in three elementary properties of $\sinh$ on $(0,\infty)$ — positivity, strict monotonicity, and surjectivity onto $(0,\infty)$ — so the constant can be characterized with no statistical mechanics at all.

A subtle but important point is that uniqueness does not actually require restricting to $\beta > 0$: because $\sinh$ is globally injective, $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$ has a unique real solution regardless of sign. The positivity hypothesis is retained because $\beta = 1/T$ is physically positive and because the squared characterization (Theorem 4.6) genuinely needs $\beta > 0$ to exclude the spurious branch $\sinh(2\beta) = -1$.

---

## 10. Future directions

The following program builds directly on the formalized self-dual point, ordered from most accessible to most ambitious.

**1. Formalize the duality map and its involutive structure.** Define the dual inverse temperature $\beta^*(\beta)$ implicitly through $\sinh(2\beta)\sinh(2\beta^*) = 1$, prove it is well defined for $\beta > 0$, and show $\beta \mapsto \beta^*$ is a continuous, strictly order-reversing involution of $(0,\infty)$ whose unique fixed point is exactly $\beta_c$. The qualitative picture of the duality — swapping high and low temperature with a single self-dual point — is captured by elementary properties of $\sinh$ on $(0,\infty)$ (positivity, strict monotonicity, range $(0,\infty)$), so the map can be built and characterized directly on top of the present results $\sinh(2\beta_c)=1$, uniqueness, and positivity/monotonicity of $\sinh$.

**2. Connect to the dual-temperature parametrization $\tanh\beta^* = e^{-2\beta}$.** Many references state the duality in the equivalent low/high-temperature form $\tanh(\beta^*) = \exp(-2\beta)$ (or $e^{-2\beta^*} = \tanh\beta$) rather than through $\sinh$. Formalize the equivalence of these parametrizations and re-derive the self-dual point from the $\tanh$ form as an independent cross-check. The $\sinh$ relation and the $\tanh$/exponential relation are two coordinates on the same one-parameter family of dualities, related by standard hyperbolic identities, so proving their equivalence is a purely analytic exercise that strengthens confidence in the constant.

**3. Build the finite-volume partition function and prove the Kramers–Wannier relation.** Define the Ising Hamiltonian and partition function on an $m\times n$ torus and prove the duality $Z(\beta) \propto Z(\beta^*)$ via the high-temperature (loop) and low-temperature (contour) expansions, thereby *deriving* relation (KW) that this work currently takes as motivation. Duality is a combinatorial bijection between even subgraphs of the lattice and domain-wall configurations of its planar dual, so the analytic constant $\beta_c$ becomes a corollary of a finite, fully discrete counting identity. With the self-dual point already formalized as the target, the combinatorics can be developed with a precise goal and validated against the known fixed point at every step.

---

## 11. Conclusion

We have given a rigorous, self-contained account of the two-dimensional Ising model's critical point, centered on the self-duality fixed-point equation $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$. The solution is the closed-form constant $\beta_c = \tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$, equivalently $T_c = 2/\log(1+\sqrt2)$, and it is the *unique* positive solution. We proved the supporting reciprocal identity $(1+\sqrt2)^{-1} = \sqrt2 - 1$, the critical value $\sinh(2\beta_c) = 1$, uniqueness via global strict monotonicity of $\sinh$, positivity of $\beta_c$, the reciprocity $T_c\beta_c = 1$, and the if-and-only-if characterization of the self-dual point through $\sinh(2\beta)^2 = 1$. Beyond its intrinsic elegance, the result is the calibration constant for an entire universality class and the simplest instance of the principle that a self-dual point locates a phase transition.

\begin{abstract}
The two-dimensional Ising model on the square lattice exhibits a continuous phase
transition separating a low-temperature ferromagnetically ordered phase from a
high-temperature disordered phase. The exact location of this transition is one of
the central results of equilibrium statistical mechanics. We give a self-contained,
rigorous account of the \emph{critical inverse temperature}
\[

characterized by the Kramers--Wannier self-duality fixed-point condition
$\sinh(2\beta) = 1$. We establish four core facts and their supporting algebraic
identities: (i) the reciprocal identity $(1+\sqrt{2})^{-1} = \sqrt{2} - 1$; (ii) the
critical value $\sinh(2\bc) = 1$; (iii) uniqueness, that any positive $\beta$ solving
$\sinh(2\beta) = 1$ equals $\bc$; and (iv) the fixed-point characterization that for
$\beta > 0$, the squared condition $\sinh(2\beta)^2 = 1$ holds if and only if
$\beta = \bc$. We additionally record the reciprocity $\Tc\,\bc = 1$ and the positivity
$\bc > 0$. The arguments rest only on elementary properties of the hyperbolic sine,
illustrating how the deep statistical-mechanical content of the duality is, at the level
of the critical point, captured by a single transcendental equation.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

The Ising model is the canonical lattice model of cooperative phenomena. It assigns to
each site of a lattice a binary spin $\sigma_i \in \{-1,+1\}$ and weights configurations
by an energy that rewards aligned neighbors. Despite its simplicity it captures the
essence of a ferromagnetic phase transition and serves as the prototype for the modern
theory of critical phenomena and universality.

In two dimensions on the square lattice the model is exactly solvable. Onsager's 1944
solution computed the free energy in closed form and revealed a divergence of the
specific heat at a sharp critical temperature. The \emph{location} of that temperature
can be pinned down by a more elementary and structurally illuminating route: the duality
of Kramers and Wannier (1941), which relates the model at inverse temperature $\beta$ to
the model at a \emph{dual} inverse temperature $\beta^*$ with hot and cold interchanged.
Granting a single transition, that transition must occur at the unique \emph{self-dual}
point, and the self-duality condition reduces to the transcendental equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:star}
  \sinh(2\beta) = 1. \tag{$\star$}
\end{equation}

This paper provides a rigorous, self-contained treatment of the constant defined by
\eqref{eq:star}. We isolate the purely analytic core of the argument---that
\eqref{eq:star} has a unique solution, given in closed form by
$\bc = \tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt{2})$---and prove it, together with the natural variants
involving the squared duality condition and the critical temperature.

\subsection{Notation}
We work over $\R$. The hyperbolic sine is $\sinh(x) = (e^x - e^{-x})/2$, with the standard
logarithm $\log$ and principal square root $\sqrt{\cdot}$. We adopt natural units in which
the nearest-neighbor coupling $J$ and Boltzmann constant $k_B$ equal $1$, so $\beta = 1/T$.

\section{Physical setting}

\subsection{The model}
Let $\Lambda \subset \Z^2$ be finite (an $m\times n$ torus). A \emph{configuration} is a
map $\sigma:\Lambda \to \{-1,+1\}$. The ferromagnetic zero-field \emph{Hamiltonian} is
\[
  H(\sigma) = -\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} \sigma_i \sigma_j,
\]
summed over nearest-neighbor pairs. The \emph{Gibbs measure} at inverse temperature
$\beta > 0$ is $P_\beta(\sigma) = Z(\beta)^{-1} e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}$ with partition
function $Z(\beta) = \sum_\sigma e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}$. The order parameter is the
magnetization $m(\beta) = \lim_{\Lambda\uparrow\Z^2}\langle\sigma_0\rangle_\beta$.

\subsection{Existence of a transition: the Peierls argument}
Deviations from the all-$+$ ground state are organized into \emph{contours}: closed domain
walls on the dual lattice. A contour of length $L$ is suppressed by $e^{-2\beta L}$, while
the number of contours of length $L$ around a fixed site grows like $C^L$. For $\beta$
large enough that $e^{-2\beta}C < 1$, the probability that a site is encircled is below
$\tfrac12$, so $\langle\sigma_0\rangle_\beta > 0$: order survives at low temperature.
Hence a critical $\bc$ exists. In one dimension the analogous defects are points whose
entropy always defeats their energy, and no transition occurs.

\subsection{Kramers--Wannier duality}
Matching the high-temperature (loop) and low-temperature (contour) expansions of $Z(\beta)$
on the square lattice yields the duality relation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kw}
  \sinh(2\beta)\,\sinh(2\beta^*) = 1, \tag{KW}
\end{equation}
under which $Z(\beta)$ and $Z(\beta^*)$ are proportional up to a smooth prefactor. The map
$\beta\mapsto\beta^*$ is a strictly order-reversing involution of $(0,\infty)$. A single
transition must sit at the self-dual point $\beta=\beta^*$, where \eqref{eq:kw} becomes
\[
  \sinh(2\beta)^2 = 1, \qquad\text{i.e. for } \beta>0,\quad \sinh(2\beta) = 1.
\]

\begin{remark}
The existence of a single transition and the derivation of \eqref{eq:kw} are statistical-
mechanical inputs. The contribution formalized here is the rigorous solution and
characterization of the self-dual equation \eqref{eq:star} and the resulting constant.
\end{remark}

\section{Definitions}

\begin{definition}[Critical inverse temperature]
$\bc := \tfrac{1}{2}\log\!\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right).$
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Critical temperature]
$\Tc := \dfrac{2}{\log\!\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right)}.$
\end{definition}

\noindent Numerically $\log(1+\sqrt2) = 0.88137358\ldots$, so $\bc = 0.44068679\ldots$ and
$\Tc = 2.26918531\ldots$.

\section{Main results}

\begin{lemma}[Reciprocal identity]\label{lem:recip}
$(1 + \sqrt{2})^{-1} = \sqrt{2} - 1.$
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Since $\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2 = 2$, $(\sqrt2-1)(1+\sqrt2) = \sqrt2 + 2 - 1 - \sqrt2 = 1$, so
$\sqrt2-1$ is the inverse of $1+\sqrt2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Critical value]\label{thm:value}
$\sinh(2\bc) = 1.$
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By definition $2\bc = \log(1+\sqrt2)$. For $x>0$, $\sinh(\log x) = (x - x^{-1})/2$. With
$x = 1+\sqrt2$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:recip},
\[
  \sinh(2\bc) = \tfrac12\big((1+\sqrt2) - (\sqrt2-1)\big) = \tfrac12\cdot 2 = 1. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness]\label{thm:unique}
If $\beta > 0$ and $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$, then $\beta = \bc$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:value}, $\sinh(2\beta) = \sinh(2\bc)$. As $\sinh' = \cosh \ge 1 > 0$,
$\sinh$ is strictly increasing, hence injective; thus $2\beta = 2\bc$ and $\beta = \bc$.
(Global injectivity makes the hypothesis $\beta>0$ unnecessary for the conclusion; it is
retained as the physical regime.)
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Positivity]\label{thm:pos}
$\bc > 0.$
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$\sqrt2 > 0 \Rightarrow 1+\sqrt2 > 1 \Rightarrow \log(1+\sqrt2) > 0$, and multiplying by
$\tfrac12$ preserves positivity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Reciprocity]\label{thm:recip}
$\Tc \cdot \bc = 1.$
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
With $L = \log(1+\sqrt2) \ne 0$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:pos}),
$\Tc\,\bc = (2/L)(L/2) = 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Self-duality fixed-point characterization]\label{thm:fix}
For $\beta > 0$, \quad $\sinh(2\beta)^2 = 1 \iff \beta = \bc.$
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) If $\beta = \bc$ then $\sinh(2\beta) = 1$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:value}, so its
square is $1$. ($\Rightarrow$) For $\beta>0$, $2\beta>0$ and $\sinh$ is positive on
$(0,\infty)$, so $s:=\sinh(2\beta)>0$. From $s^2=1$ and $s>0$ we get $s=1$; the root $-1$ is
excluded. Theorem~\ref{thm:unique} gives $\beta=\bc$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:fix} is the precise sense in which ``critical'' and ``self-dual'' coincide.

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Closed-form evaluation}
Evaluate the closed forms of the definitions in floating point and verify
$\sinh(2\bc)=1$ to machine precision; $O(1)$ cost.

\subsection{Root-finding cross-check via bisection}
$f(\beta) = \sinh(2\beta) - 1$ is continuous and strictly increasing with $f(0) = -1 < 0$ and

error below $2^{-n}$ after $n$ steps; the root matches $\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$.

\subsection{Duality involution and its fixed point}
With \eqref{eq:kw}, the dual map is
$\beta^*(\beta) = \tfrac12\operatorname{arcsinh}(1/\sinh(2\beta))$. Verifying
$\beta^*\circ\beta^* = \mathrm{id}$ and $\beta^*(\bc)=\bc$ provides a structural check.

\section{Applications and significance}

The 2D Ising critical point is the reference standard for critical phenomena, calibrating
Monte Carlo simulations, finite-size scaling, and series expansions. Through the lattice-gas
correspondence ($\sigma_i = 2n_i - 1$) it equals the liquid--vapor and binary-alloy critical
points. Kramers--Wannier duality is the historical seed of order/disorder duality and of the
broad principle that a self-dual point pins a phase transition; \eqref{eq:star} is its simplest
nontrivial instance.

\section{Discussion}

The treatment separates two layers. The physical layer---existence and uniqueness of the
transition (Peierls) and the duality relation \eqref{eq:kw}---supplies the reason the critical
point coincides with the self-dual point. The analytic layer---solving \eqref{eq:star}---is what
we have made fully rigorous: the closed form $\bc=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$, its uniqueness via
strict monotonicity of $\sinh$, the positivity of $\sinh$ on $(0,\infty)$ that promotes
$\sinh^2=1$ to $\sinh=1$, and the reciprocity $\Tc\bc=1$. Uniqueness does not in fact require
$\beta>0$, since $\sinh$ is globally injective; positivity is retained as the physical regime and
because Theorem~\ref{thm:fix} needs it to exclude the spurious branch $\sinh(2\beta)=-1$.

\section{Future directions}

\paragraph{1. Formalize the duality map and its involutive structure.}
Define $\beta^*(\beta)$ implicitly via $\sinh(2\beta)\sinh(2\beta^*)=1$, prove it is well
defined for $\beta>0$, and show $\beta\mapsto\beta^*$ is a continuous, strictly order-reversing
involution of $(0,\infty)$ with unique fixed point $\bc$. The qualitative duality picture is
captured by elementary properties of $\sinh$ on $(0,\infty)$ (positivity, strict monotonicity,
range $(0,\infty)$), so the map builds directly on the present results.

\paragraph{2. Connect to the parametrization $\tanh\beta^* = e^{-2\beta}$.}
Formalize the equivalence of the $\sinh$ form and the low/high-temperature form
$\tanh(\beta^*) = \exp(-2\beta)$, and re-derive the self-dual point from the $\tanh$ form as an
independent cross-check, using standard hyperbolic identities.

\paragraph{3. Build the finite-volume partition function and prove (KW).}
Define the Hamiltonian and partition function on an $m\times n$ torus and prove
$Z(\beta)\propto Z(\beta^*)$ via the high- and low-temperature expansions, deriving \eqref{eq:kw}.
Duality is a combinatorial bijection between even subgraphs and dual domain walls, so $\bc$
becomes a corollary of a finite counting identity, validated against the known fixed point.

\section{Conclusion}

We gave a rigorous, self-contained account of the 2D Ising critical point, centered on the
self-duality equation $\sinh(2\beta)=1$. Its unique positive solution is
$\bc=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$, equivalently $\Tc=2/\log(1+\sqrt2)$. We proved the reciprocal
identity $(1+\sqrt2)^{-1}=\sqrt2-1$, the critical value $\sinh(2\bc)=1$, uniqueness via strict
monotonicity, positivity, the reciprocity $\Tc\bc=1$, and the iff characterization through
$\sinh(2\beta)^2=1$. The result is the calibration constant for an entire universality class and
the simplest instance of the principle that a self-dual point locates a phase transition.

# The Ising Model Critical Temperature

This file formalizes the critical inverse temperature `βc = (1/2) log(1 + √2)`
of the two-dimensional Ising model, characterized by the Kramers–Wannier
self-duality fixed point condition `sinh(2β) = 1`.

namespace IsingCriticalTemperature

open Real

/-- The critical inverse temperature of the 2D Ising model. -/
noncomputable def isingBetaC : ℝ := (1 / 2) * log (1 + sqrt 2)

/-- The critical temperature of the 2D Ising model. -/
noncomputable def isingTc : ℝ := 2 / log (1 + sqrt 2)

/-- The reciprocal of `1 + √2` equals `√2 - 1`. -/
theorem inv_one_add_sqrt_two : (1 + sqrt 2)⁻¹ = sqrt 2 - 1 := by
  have hs : sqrt 2 * sqrt 2 = 2 := Real.mul_self_sqrt (by norm_num)
  refine inv_eq_of_mul_eq_one_left ?_
  nlinarith [hs]

/-- At the critical inverse temperature, `sinh(2βc) = 1`. -/
theorem sinh_two_isingBetaC : sinh (2 * isingBetaC) = 1 := by
  have hx : (0 : ℝ) < 1 + sqrt 2 := by positivity
  have he : 2 * isingBetaC = log (1 + sqrt 2) := by unfold isingBetaC; ring
  rw [he, Real.sinh_log hx, inv_one_add_sqrt_two]
  ring

/-- The critical inverse temperature is the unique positive solution of
`sinh(2β) = 1`. The hypothesis `0 < β` is kept as part of the intended
statement, but it turns out to be unnecessary since `sinh` is injective on
all of `ℝ`. -/
theorem isingBetaC_unique {β : ℝ} (hβ : 0 < β) (h : sinh (2 * β) = 1) :
    β = isingBetaC := by
  have heq : sinh (2 * β) = sinh (2 * isingBetaC) := by
    rw [h, sinh_two_isingBetaC]
  have h2 : 2 * β = 2 * isingBetaC := Real.sinh_strictMono.injective heq
  linarith

/-- The critical inverse temperature is positive. -/
theorem isingBetaC_pos : 0 < isingBetaC := by
  have h1 : (1 : ℝ) < 1 + sqrt 2 := by
    have := Real.sqrt_pos.mpr (show (0 : ℝ) < 2 by norm_num)
    linarith
  have hl : 0 < log (1 + sqrt 2) := Real.log_pos h1
  unfold isingBetaC
  positivity

/-- The product of the critical temperature and critical inverse temperature
is `1`. -/
theorem isingTc_mul_isingBetaC : isingTc * isingBetaC = 1 := by
  have h1 : (1 : ℝ) < 1 + sqrt 2 := by
    have := Real.sqrt_pos.mpr (show (0 : ℝ) < 2 by norm_num)
    linarith
  have hl : log (1 + sqrt 2) ≠ 0 := ne_of_gt (Real.log_pos h1)
  unfold isingTc isingBetaC
  field_simp

/-- The Kramers–Wannier self-duality fixed point: for `β > 0`, the condition
`sinh(2β)² = 1` holds iff `β` is the critical inverse temperature. -/
theorem dual_fixed_point_iff {β : ℝ} (hβ : 0 < β) :
    sinh (2 * β) ^ 2 = 1 ↔ β = isingBetaC := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    have hpos : 0 < sinh (2 * β) :=
      Mathlib.Meta.Positivity.sinh_pos_of_pos (by linarith)
    have h1 : sinh (2 * β) = 1 := by nlinarith [h, hpos]
    exact isingBetaC_unique hβ h1
  · intro h
    subst h
    simp [sinh_two_isingBetaC]

end IsingCriticalTemperature

Numerical demonstrations for the 2D Ising model critical point.

This script reproduces, in floating point, the algebraic facts proved formally:

  * Definition:  beta_c = (1/2) * log(1 + sqrt(2))
                 T_c    = 2 / log(1 + sqrt(2))

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core closed-form constants
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def ising_beta_c() -> float:
    """Critical inverse temperature beta_c = (1/2) * log(1 + sqrt(2))."""
    return 0.5 * math.log(1.0 + math.sqrt(2.0))


def ising_T_c() -> float:
    """Critical temperature T_c = 2 / log(1 + sqrt(2))."""
    return 2.0 / math.log(1.0 + math.sqrt(2.0))

# Demonstration 1: closed-form values and reciprocity T_c * beta_c = 1

    print(f"  beta_c > 0  (isingBetaC_pos): {beta_c > 0.0}")
    print(f"  T_c * beta_c = {T_c * beta_c:.15f}  (should be 1.0)")
    print(f"  reciprocity holds: {math.isclose(T_c * beta_c, 1.0, rel_tol=1e-12)}")
    print()

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def demo_defining_identity() -> None:

    print(f"  sinh_two_isingBetaC: {math.isclose(s, 1.0, abs_tol=1e-12)}")
    print()

    print()

def bisection_root(
    f: Callable[[float], float], lo: float, hi: float, iters: int = 80
) -> float:
    """Bisection root finder for a continuous, strictly increasing f on [lo, hi]."""
    flo = f(lo)
    for _ in range(iters):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        fmid = f(mid)
        if (fmid > 0.0) == (flo > 0.0):
            lo, flo = mid, fmid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)

## Research Brief: Combinatorial Number Theory — Binomial Coefficients and Prime Bounds

### Objective
Formalize and prove a chain of results that bridges combinatorics and analytic number theory, deriving prime distribution bounds from binomial coefficient properties.

### Key Definitions
- `v_p (n p : ℕ) : ℕ` — the p-adic valuation of n (exponent of prime p in factorization of n)
- `central_binom (n : ℕ) : ℕ := Nat.choose (2*n) n` — the central binomial coefficient
- `prime_product_below (n : ℕ) : ℕ` — product of all primes p ≤ n

### Main Theorems to Prove

**Theorem 1 (Legendre's formula — p-adic valuation of factorials):**
`v_p (n!) p = (n - s_p(n)) / (p - 1)`
where `s_p(n)` is the sum of digits of n in base p. At minimum, prove the corollary:
`v_p (C(2n,n)) p = (s_p(n) + s_p(n) - s_p(2n)) / (p-1)`
and derive: for prime p with n < p ≤ 2n, `v_p (C(2n,n)) p = 1`.

**Theorem 2 (Central binomial coefficient bounds):**
Prove that `4^n / (2n+1) ≤ C(2n,n) ≤ 4^n / (2√n)` for n ≥ 1.
The lower bound follows from `C(2n,n) = (2n)!/(n!)^2` and induction or direct computation. The upper bound requires more care.

**Theorem 3 (Chebyshev's product bound — the bridge result):**
`∏_{p prime, p ≤ n} p < 4^n` for all n ≥ 1.

**Proof strategy for Theorem 3:**
- By Theorem 1, every prime p with n < p ≤ 2n divides C(2n,n) exactly once.
- Therefore: `∏_{p ≤ 2n} p ≤ C(2n,n) × ∏_{p ≤ n} p × ∏_{p ≤ n/2} p × ...`
- Alternatively, use the cleaner argument: `∏_{n < p ≤ 2n} p ≤ C(2n,n) ≤ 4^n`.
- Then prove by strong induction on n that `∏_{p ≤ n} p < 4^n`.

### Auxiliary Results Needed
- `Nat.choose (2*n) n ≥ 2^n / (2*n + 1)` (lower bound on central binomial coefficient)
- For prime p and n < p ≤ 2n: `p ∣ Nat.choose (2*n) n` (divisibility of central binomial coefficient by primes in (n, 2n])
- `v_p (n!) p = ∑_{i≥1} ⌊n/p^i⌋` (Legendre's formula, standard form)

### Constraints
- Do NOT just call existing Mathlib theorems as black boxes. The proofs should reveal the bridge structure.
- Each theorem should be proved from more primitive results, making the cross-domain connections explicit.
- The p-adic valuation results must use the combinatorial structure of binomial coefficients, not just algebraic properties of Z.
- The final Chebyshev bound must be derived FROM the binomial coefficient bounds, not proved independently.

### Significance
This is a genuine bridge: combinatorial identities about binomial coefficients (a purely enumerative topic) imply distributional results about primes (an analytic number theory topic). The proof path cannot stay within one domain. This formalizes a famous argument of Erdős.

/-! # A Custom Number-Theory Decision Tactic and Its Soundness

This file defines a small custom tactic, `number_theory_decide`, intended as a
convenient front-end for closing simple decidable / arithmetic number-theoretic
goals.  It then establishes the soundness of the `decide` core (the only branch
that relies on `Decidable` evaluation) and proves three genuine
number-theoretic theorems *without* using the custom tactic.

The custom tactic is purely a convenience combinator: each of its branches
(`omega`, `decide`, `norm_num`, `simp_all`) produces a kernel-checked proof
term, so the tactic is sound exactly when these underlying tactics are.  The
soundness theorem below records the key fact behind the `decide` branch.
-/

namespace Bridges.ProofAutomation

/-! ## 1. Custom tactic definition

`number_theory_decide` tries, in order, `omega`, `decide`, `norm_num`, and
`simp_all`, succeeding as soon as one of them closes the goal. -/

macro "number_theory_decide" : tactic =>
  `(tactic| first
    | omega
    | decide
    | norm_num
    | simp_all)

/-! ## 2. Soundness of the `decide` branch

The only branch of `number_theory_decide` that depends on evaluating a
`Decidable` instance is `decide`.  Its soundness is exactly the standard
Mathlib lemma `of_decide_eq_true`: if `decide p` evaluates to `true`, then `p`
holds.  The other branches (`omega`, `norm_num`, `simp_all`) emit ordinary
kernel-checked proof terms and so need no separate soundness statement. -/

theorem number_theory_decide_sound (p : Prop) [Decidable p]
    (h : decide p = true) : p :=
  of_decide_eq_true h

/-! ## 3. Three number-theoretic theorems (proved WITHOUT `number_theory_decide`) -/

/-- The product of any three consecutive natural numbers is divisible by `6`.

    The product is divisible by `6` exactly when it vanishes modulo `6`; we reduce
    the goal to `n % 6` and check the six residues. -/
theorem six_dvd_consecutive_three (n : ℕ) : 6 ∣ n * (n + 1) * (n + 2) := by

# Future Directions — Proof Automation: Custom Lean 4 Tactics

Derived from the Stage 3 (Analysis) and Stage 4 (Critique) findings of this
cycle (`TropicalSimp.lean`, `NumberTheoryDecide.lean`, `SpectralBound.lean`).

## 1. A confluent, terminating `tropical_simp` normal form
**Conjecture.** The min-plus rewrite system underlying `tropical_simp`
(scalar distributivity + idempotent commutative monoid laws of `min`) is
confluent and terminating, so every min-plus expression has a *unique* normal
form: a single `min` over affine monomials with no repeated exponents.
**The key insight is** that min-plus distributivity pushes every `+` past every
`min`, after which idempotency (`min_self`) deduplicates monomials — exactly the
canonicalisation already proved for tropical polynomials in `Tropical/Core`.
**Why now?** This cycle proved the distributive backbone (`tropical_fold_distrib`,
`tropical_inf'_distrib`); a termination measure (multiset of `+`-depths) is now
within reach and would turn `tropical_simp` into a decision procedure for
min-plus equality.

## 2. `number_theory_decide` as a residue-class reflection tactic
**Conjecture.** Every universally-quantified statement of the form
`∀ n, P (n % m)` with `P` decidable is provably equivalent to the finite check
`∀ r < m, P r`, and this reduction can be automated soundly.
**The key insight is** that `n % m` ranges over exactly `{0, …, m-1}`, so the
unbounded universal collapses to a `decide`-able finite disjunction — the same
parity move used in `sq_mod_four`, generalised from `m = 2,4` to arbitrary `m`.
**Why now?** `sq_mod_four` showed the two-case instance; lifting it to a
`Fin m`-indexed reflection lemma would let `number_theory_decide` settle a whole
class of Catalog quadratic-residue and divisibility facts in one line.

## 3. Column-sum and symmetric-matrix sharpenings of `spectral_bound`
**Conjecture.** For Hermitian `A`, the eigenvalue bound
`‖μ‖ ≤ ⨆ i, ∑ j ‖A i j‖` can be strengthened to a two-sided real interval
`[λ_min, λ_max]` contained in the union of Gershgorin discs, with the discs
centred on real diagonal entries.
**The key insight is** that Hermitian matrices have real spectra and equal row /
column sums for the modulus, so the existential `eigenvalue_norm_le_row_sum`
becomes a genuine interval localisation rather than a modulus bound.
**Why now?** This cycle established the modulus bound from Gershgorin; Mathlib
already carries the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices, so the interval
refinement only needs to glue the two existing results.

## 4. Tropical eigenvalue (max-plus) bridge to `spectral_bound`
**Conjecture.** The tropical (min-plus) eigenvalue of a square matrix — the
minimum cycle mean — admits a Gershgorin-style localisation
`λ_trop ≥ ⨅ i, A i i` analogous to `eigenvalue_norm_le_max_row_sum`.
**The key insight is** that min-plus matrix powers compute shortest paths, so the
tropical eigenvalue is a min over cycle means, and the diagonal entries are the
length-1 cycles bounding it — directly reusing `tropical_inf'_distrib`.
**Why now?** With both a verified min-plus distributive calculus (File I) and a
verified classical spectral bound (File III) in hand, the max-plus eigenvalue is
the natural bridge object unifying the two automation themes.

## 5. A unified soundness meta-theorem for `simp`-set tactics
**Conjecture.** Any tactic defined as `simp only [L]` for a list `L` of proved
equational lemmas is sound by construction, and this can be packaged as a
reusable Lean attribute that certifies new domain tactics automatically.
**The key insight is** that soundness of such tactics is *not* a per-tactic
theorem but a corollary of `simp` emitting kernel-checked terms — so the audit
reduces to checking each member of `L` is a `theorem`, which is mechanisable.
**Why now?** All three tactics in this cycle share the identical soundness
argument; abstracting it would let the Catalog add domain tactics with a single
certified template instead of bespoke soundness prose.

-- NEW_FILE: Catalog/Physics/HamiltonianCompression.lean
import Mathlib

/-!
# Hamiltonian Compression Factor of Cubic Edge-Transitive Graphs

This file investigates the **Hamiltonian compression factor** `κ(Γ)` of cubic
(`3`-regular) edge-transitive graphs.  A Hamiltonian cycle `C` of a graph `Γ`
on `n` vertices is **`2`-symmetric** when there is an automorphism `g` of `Γ`
of order `2` that acts on `C` as the rotation by `n/2` positions; the conjecture
under study (supported by exhaustive computation up to `10 000` vertices) states
that every Hamiltonian connected cubic edge-transitive graph admits such a cycle,
i.e. `κ(Γ) ≥ 2`.

We make the combinatorial heart of this phenomenon fully rigorous through the
family of **Möbius ladders** `ML m`, the circulant graphs on `ZMod (2*m)` with
connection set `{±1, m}`.  These are cubic, contain the canonical Hamiltonian
cycle `0,1,…,2m-1`, and carry the half–rotation `x ↦ x + m` as an automorphism
of order `2` acting on that cycle as a rotation by exactly `n/2 = m`.  For
`m = 2` this graph is `K₄` and for `m = 3` it is `K₃,₃`; both are genuine cubic
edge-transitive Hamiltonian graphs, so the construction realises `κ ≥ 2` for
them concretely.

We also prove the structural reason the statement "rotation by `n/2`" even makes
sense: by the handshaking lemma **every cubic graph has an even number of
vertices**.

## Main results

* `HamCompression.cubic_even_order` — every cubic graph has even order
  (handshaking lemma; the parity ground for "rotation by `n/2`").
* `HamCompression.halfAut` — the half rotation `x ↦ x + m` is an automorphism
  of the Möbius ladder `ML m`.
* `HamCompression.halfAut_involutive`, `HamCompression.halfAut_ne_id` — the
  automorphism has order exactly `2`.
* `HamCompression.mobiusLadder_twoSymHamCycle` — `ML m` admits a `2`-symmetric
  Hamiltonian cycle for every `m ≥ 1`, i.e. `κ(ML m) ≥ 2`.
* `HamCompression.K4_twoSym`, `HamCompression.K33_twoSym` — the concrete cubic
  edge-transitive instances `K₄ = ML 2` and `K₃,₃ = ML 3`.
* `HamCompression.ML_degree_two`, `HamCompression.ML_degree_three` — the
  cubicity of these instances.

## Reference catalog topics

`math.CO/graph_theory/{hamiltonian_cycles, symmetric_graphs, cubic_graphs}`.
-/

open SimpleGraph

namespace HamCompression

/-! ## The handshaking ground: cubic graphs have even order -/

/-- **Handshaking corollary.** A finite cubic (`3`-regular) graph has an even
number of vertices.  Hence "rotation by `n/2`" is always well defined for the
graphs in scope.  The proof uses `∑ degrees = 2·#edges`. -/
theorem cubic_even_order {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (h : ∀ v, G.degree v = 3) :
    Even (Fintype.card V) := by
  have hsum := G.sum_degrees_eq_twice_card_edges
  have hl : ∑ v, G.degree v = 3 * Fintype.card V := by
    simp only [h, Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, smul_eq_mul]
    ring
  rw [hl] at hsum
  -- 3 * card V = 2 * E  ⇒  card V even
  have h2 : 2 ∣ Fintype.card V := by omega
  obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h2
  exact ⟨k, by omega⟩

/-! ## The Möbius ladder circulant `ML m` -/

/-- The Möbius ladder on `ZMod (2*m)`: vertices joined to their cyclic
neighbours `x ± 1` and to the antipode `x + m`.  `ML 2 = K₄`, `ML 3 = K₃,₃`. -/
def ML (m : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (ZMod (2 * m)) :=
  SimpleGraph.fromRel (fun a b : ZMod (2 * m) => b = a + 1 ∨ b = a + m)

/-- Adjacency in `ML m` unfolded. -/
theorem ML_adj_iff (m : ℕ) (x y : ZMod (2 * m)) :
    (ML m).Adj x y ↔
      x ≠ y ∧ ((y = x + 1 ∨ y = x + m) ∨ (x = y + 1 ∨ x = y + m)) := Iff.rfl

instance ML.decidableAdj (m : ℕ) : DecidableRel (ML m).Adj :=
  fun a b => decidable_of_iff _ (ML_adj_iff m a b).symm

/-- The cyclic edge `i — (i+1)` belongs to `ML m` when `m ≥ 1`. -/
theorem ML_cycle_edge (m : ℕ) (hm : 1 ≤ m) (i : ZMod (2 * m)) :
    (ML m).Adj i (i + 1) := by
  rw [ML_adj_iff]
  refine ⟨?_, Or.inl (Or.inl rfl)⟩
  -- i ≠ i + 1 since 1 ≠ 0 in ZMod (2*m) with 2*m ≥ 2
  intro hcon
  have h1 : (1 : ZMod (2 * m)) = 0 := by linear_combination -hcon
  have : ((1 : ℕ) : ZMod (2 * m)) = 0 := by exact_mod_cast h1
  rw [ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff] at this
  have := Nat.le_of_dvd (by norm_num) this
  omega

/-! ## The half–rotation automorphism -/

/-- The half rotation `x ↦ x + m` is an automorphism of `ML m`: it permutes the
connection set `{±1, m}` to itself.  This is the order-`2` symmetry that
"compresses" the Hamiltonian cycle. -/
noncomputable def halfAut (m : ℕ) : ML m ≃g ML m where
  toEquiv := Equiv.addRight (m : ZMod (2 * m))
  map_rel_iff' := by
    intro x y
    simp only [ML, Equiv.coe_addRight, SimpleGraph.fromRel_adj]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨hne, h⟩
      refine ⟨by simpa using hne, ?_⟩
      rcases h with (h | h) | (h | h)
      · exact Or.inl (Or.inl (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inl (Or.inr (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inr (Or.inl (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inr (Or.inr (by linear_combination h))
    · rintro ⟨hne, h⟩
      refine ⟨by simpa using hne, ?_⟩
      rcases h with (h | h) | (h | h)
      · exact Or.inl (Or.inl (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inl (Or.inr (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inr (Or.inl (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inr (Or.inr (by linear_combination h))

@[simp] theorem halfAut_apply (m : ℕ) (x : ZMod (2 * m)) :
    halfAut m x = x + m := rfl

/-- The half rotation is an involution: applying it twice is the identity. -/
theorem halfAut_involutive (m : ℕ) :
    (halfAut m).toEquiv.trans (halfAut m).toEquiv = Equiv.refl _ := by
  have hmm : (m : ZMod (2 * m)) + m = 0 := by
    have : ((2 * m : ℕ) : ZMod (2 * m)) = 0 := ZMod.natCast_self (2 * m)
    push_cast at this; linear_combination this
  ext z
  simp only [Equiv.trans_apply, halfAut, Equiv.coe_addRight, Equiv.refl_apply]
  linear_combination hmm

/-- The half rotation is not the identity (so it has order exactly `2`) whenever
`m ≥ 1`. -/
theorem halfAut_ne_id (m : ℕ) (hm : 1 ≤ m) :
    (halfAut m).toEquiv ≠ Equiv.refl _ := by
  intro hcon
  have h0 := Equiv.ext_iff.mp hcon 0
  simp only [halfAut, Equiv.coe_addRight, Equiv.refl_apply, zero_add] at h0
  have : ((m : ℕ) : ZMod (2 * m)) ≠ 0 := by
    rw [Ne, ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff]
    intro hdvd
    have := Nat.le_of_dvd (by omega) hdvd
    omega
  exact this h0

/-! ## `2`-symmetric Hamiltonian cycles and the compression factor -/

/-- A graph `G` admits a **`2`-symmetric Hamiltonian cycle** (`κ(G) ≥ 2`) when
there is a cyclic enumeration `c : ZMod n ≃ V` of all vertices whose successive
vertices are adjacent (a Hamiltonian cycle), together with an automorphism `g`
of order `2` acting on the cycle as the rotation by `n/2` positions. -/
def HasTwoSymHamCycle {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ (n : ℕ) (_ : Fintype.card V = n) (c : ZMod n ≃ V) (g : G ≃g G),
    (∀ i : ZMod n, G.Adj (c i) (c (i + 1))) ∧
    (g.toEquiv.trans g.toEquiv = Equiv.refl V) ∧
    (g.toEquiv ≠ Equiv.refl V) ∧
    (∀ i : ZMod n, g (c i) = c (i + (n / 2 : ℕ)))

/-- **Main construction.** For every `m ≥ 1` the Möbius ladder `ML m` admits a
`2`-symmetric Hamiltonian cycle, i.e. its Hamiltonian compression factor
satisfies `κ(ML m) ≥ 2`.  The cycle is `0,1,…,2m-1` and the symmetry is the
half rotation `x ↦ x + m`, which acts on the cycle as the rotation by
`n/2 = m`. -/
theorem mobiusLadder_twoSymHamCycle (m : ℕ) (hm : 1 ≤ m) [NeZero (2 * m)] :
    HasTwoSymHamCycle (ML m) := by
  refine ⟨2 * m, ZMod.card (2 * m), Equiv.refl _, halfAut m, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro i; exact ML_cycle_edge m hm i
  · exact halfAut_involutive m
  · exact halfAut_ne_id m hm
  · intro i
    simp only [Equiv.refl_apply, halfAut_apply]
    -- need : i + m = i + ((2*m)/2 : ℕ) in ZMod (2*m); and (2*m)/2 = m
    have h2 : (2 * m) / 2 = m := by omega
    rw [h2]

/-! ## Concrete cubic edge-transitive instances -/

/-- `ML 2 = K₄` admits a `2`-symmetric Hamiltonian cycle. -/
theorem K4_twoSym : HasTwoSymHamCycle (ML 2) :=
  mobiusLadder_twoSymHamCycle 2 (by norm_num)

/-- `ML 3 = K₃,₃` admits a `2`-symmetric Hamiltonian cycle. -/
theorem K33_twoSym : HasTwoSymHamCycle (ML 3) :=
  mobiusLadder_twoSymHamCycle 3 (by norm_num)

/-- `ML 2` (`= K₄`) is cubic: every vertex has degree `3`. -/
theorem ML_degree_two : ∀ v : ZMod (2 * 2), (ML 2).degree v = 3 := by decide

/-- `ML 3` (`= K₃,₃`) is cubic: every vertex has degree `3`. -/
theorem ML_degree_three : ∀ v : ZMod (2 * 3), (ML 3).degree v = 3 := by decide

/-! ## Consistency check: cubicity ⇒ even order, realised on the instances -/

/-- The order of `ML 2` is even, consistent with `cubic_even_order`. -/
theorem ML2_even_order : Even (Fintype.card (ZMod (2 * 2))) :=
  cubic_even_order (ML 2) ML_degree_two

/-- The order of `ML 3` is even, consistent with `cubic_even_order`. -/
theorem ML3_even_order : Even (Fintype.card (ZMod (2 * 3))) :=
  cubic_even_order (ML 3) ML_degree_three

/-
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

Hypothesis (Hypothesizer).
  H1.  Every Hamiltonian connected cubic edge-transitive graph has κ ≥ 2
       (a 2-symmetric Hamiltonian cycle).  [the headline conjecture]
  H2.  The half rotation x ↦ x + n/2 of a circulant cycle is *always* a graph
       automorphism of order 2 — the universal mechanism producing κ ≥ 2.
  H3.  (surprising) "Hamiltonian" cannot be dropped: there are cubic
       edge-transitive graphs with NO Hamiltonian cycle at all, so κ is
       undefined for them.  The Petersen graph is the smallest such graph.
  H4.  (surprising) "rotation by n/2" forces n even — but this is automatic:
       every cubic graph has even order, so the index n/2 is never a fudge.
  H5.  K₄ and K₃,₃ are the two smallest cubic edge-transitive graphs and both
       are realised as Möbius ladders ML 2, ML 3.

Experiment (Experimenter).
  * H2 was proved in full generality: `halfAut`, `halfAut_involutive`,
    `halfAut_ne_id`.  The decisive computation is that x ↦ x+m sends the
    connection set {+1, +m, -1, -m} to itself; `linear_combination` discharges
    each of the eight adjacency-preservation cases.
  * H1 restricted to the realisable circulant family is
    `mobiusLadder_twoSymHamCycle`; for the concrete edge-transitive instances
    K₄ and K₃,₃ it specialises to `K4_twoSym`, `K33_twoSym`.
  * H4 was proved as `cubic_even_order` via the handshaking lemma
    `sum_degrees_eq_twice_card_edges` and an `omega` parity argument.
  * H5 / cubicity verified by `ML_degree_two`, `ML_degree_three`.

Analysis (Analyst).
  * SURVIVED: H2 (universal, generic m), H4 (handshaking), H5, and H1 on the
    Möbius-ladder family including the two smallest edge-transitive cubic
    graphs.  These are "true and provable now".
  * "TRUE BUT HARD": H1 in *full* generality (all cubic edge-transitive graphs
    up to 10 000 vertices).  This needs a classification of cubic edge-transitive
    graphs plus an existence proof of a σ-invariant Hamiltonian cycle; the
    classification is not in Mathlib.  Our family captures the mechanism but not
    the classification.
  * "NEEDS A DIFFERENT DEFINITION": stating κ via Mathlib's
    `Walk.IsHamiltonianCycle` is awkward because the rotation action is most
    naturally phrased on the *cyclic index* `ZMod n`.  We therefore encoded a
    Hamiltonian cycle as a bijection `ZMod n ≃ V` with adjacent successors; this

Critique / Adversarial review (Critic).
  * Counterexample hunt for H2: is x ↦ x+m ever NOT order 2?  Only if m = 0
    (n = 0).  Guarded by `hm : 1 ≤ m`; `halfAut_ne_id` shows it is a genuine
    involution, never the identity, so order is exactly 2.  Robust.
  * Counterexample to "drop Hamiltonicity" (H3): the Petersen graph is cubic and
    edge-transitive but NOT Hamiltonian, so it has no Hamiltonian cycle and κ is

    `linear_combination` over `ZMod`.  `ML_degree_two/three` are decidable
    instance checks used only as *supporting* cubicity facts, never as the main

  * Hidden corner case: does "rotation by n/2" require n even?  Yes — and

Synthesis (Principal Investigator).
  The compression-factor phenomenon for the realisable circulant family reduces
  to one clean algebraic fact: translation by n/2 is an order-2 automorphism

  cycle by exactly half.  The two smallest cubic edge-transitive graphs (K₄,

-/

import Physics.HamiltonianCompression

/-!
# Boundary analysis of the Hamiltonian compression factor

This companion file sharpens the results of `HamiltonianCompression.lean` by
nailing down *why* the half rotation realises the compression factor and *where*
the headline conjecture's hypotheses become load-bearing.

## Main results

* `HamCompression.halfAut_fixedPointFree` — the half rotation moves every
  vertex; it is a fixed-point-free involution, hence it partitions the `2m`
  vertices into `m` antipodal pairs.
* `HamCompression.halfAut_orderOf` — in the automorphism group, the half
  rotation has order **exactly** `2`.  This is the precise statement
  "automorphism `g` of order `2`" from the definition of `κ ≥ 2`.
* `HamCompression.odd_order_not_cubic` — adversarial necessity of even order:
  no graph of odd order is cubic (contrapositive of `cubic_even_order`).
* `HamCompression.fullRot` / `HamCompression.fullRot_not_half` — the *full*
  rotation `x ↦ x + 1` is also an automorphism, but it does **not** act on the
  cycle as a rotation by `n/2`; this shows compression requires choosing the
  right symmetry, not just any automorphism.

## Reference catalog topics

`math.CO/graph_theory/{hamiltonian_cycles, symmetric_graphs, cubic_graphs}`.
-/

open SimpleGraph

namespace HamCompression

/-! ## The half rotation is a fixed-point-free involution -/

/-- The half rotation `x ↦ x + m` moves every vertex (`m ≥ 1`).  Together with
`halfAut_involutive` this says it is a fixed-point-free involution: it splits
the `2m` vertices into `m` antipodal pairs `{x, x+m}`. -/
theorem halfAut_fixedPointFree (m : ℕ) (hm : 1 ≤ m) (x : ZMod (2 * m)) :
    halfAut m x ≠ x := by
  rw [halfAut_apply]
  intro h
  have hne : ((m : ℕ) : ZMod (2 * m)) ≠ 0 := by
    rw [Ne, ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff]
    intro hdvd
    have := Nat.le_of_dvd (by omega) hdvd
    omega
  exact hne (by linear_combination h)

/-! ## The half rotation has order exactly two in the automorphism group -/

/-- **Order exactly two.** In the automorphism group `ML m ≃g ML m`, the half
rotation `halfAut m` has order `2`.  This is the exact meaning of "automorphism
`g` of order `2`" in the definition of compression factor `κ ≥ 2`. -/
theorem halfAut_orderOf (m : ℕ) (hm : 1 ≤ m) [NeZero (2 * m)] :
    orderOf (halfAut m) = 2 := by
  have hmm : (m : ZMod (2 * m)) + m = 0 := by
    have : ((2 * m : ℕ) : ZMod (2 * m)) = 0 := ZMod.natCast_self (2 * m)
    push_cast at this; linear_combination this
  apply orderOf_eq_prime
  · -- (halfAut m) ^ 2 = 1
    ext z
    show (halfAut m) ((halfAut m) z) = z
    simp only [halfAut_apply]
    linear_combination hmm
  · -- halfAut m ≠ 1
    intro hcon
    have hz := RelIso.ext_iff.mp hcon 0
    have hne : ((m : ℕ) : ZMod (2 * m)) ≠ 0 := by
      rw [Ne, ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff]
      intro hdvd
      have := Nat.le_of_dvd (by omega) hdvd
      omega
    apply hne
    have hz0 : (halfAut m) 0 = (1 : ML m ≃g ML m) 0 := hz
    simp only [halfAut_apply, zero_add] at hz0
    simpa using hz0

/-! ## Adversarial necessity of even order -/

/-- **Adversarial / necessity.** A graph of odd order cannot be cubic.  This is
the contrapositive of `cubic_even_order` and shows the parity hypothesis behind
"rotation by `n/2`" is forced, never assumed. -/
theorem odd_order_not_cubic {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hodd : ¬ Even (Fintype.card V)) :
    ¬ (∀ v, G.degree v = 3) := fun h => hodd (cubic_even_order G h)

/-! ## The full rotation: an automorphism that is *not* a half rotation -/

/-- The full rotation `x ↦ x + 1` is also an automorphism of `ML m` (the
cycle's rotational symmetry). -/
noncomputable def fullRot (m : ℕ) : ML m ≃g ML m where
  toEquiv := Equiv.addRight (1 : ZMod (2 * m))
  map_rel_iff' := by
    intro x y
    simp only [ML, Equiv.coe_addRight, SimpleGraph.fromRel_adj]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨hne, h⟩
      refine ⟨by simpa using hne, ?_⟩
      rcases h with (h | h) | (h | h)
      · exact Or.inl (Or.inl (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inl (Or.inr (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inr (Or.inl (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inr (Or.inr (by linear_combination h))
    · rintro ⟨hne, h⟩
      refine ⟨by simpa using hne, ?_⟩
      rcases h with (h | h) | (h | h)
      · exact Or.inl (Or.inl (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inl (Or.inr (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inr (Or.inl (by linear_combination h))
      · exact Or.inr (Or.inr (by linear_combination h))

@[simp] theorem fullRot_apply (m : ℕ) (x : ZMod (2 * m)) :
    fullRot m x = x + 1 := rfl

/-- **Adversarial witness.** For `m ≥ 2` the full rotation `x ↦ x + 1` is an
automorphism that does *not* act on the canonical Hamiltonian cycle as a
rotation by `n/2 = m`: it sends position `0` to position `1 ≠ m`.  Hence
"`κ ≥ 2`" genuinely needs the *half* rotation, not an arbitrary automorphism. -/
theorem fullRot_not_half (m : ℕ) (hm : 2 ≤ m) :
    fullRot m 0 ≠ halfAut m 0 := by
  simp only [fullRot_apply, halfAut_apply, zero_add]
  -- (1 : ZMod (2*m)) ≠ (m : ZMod (2*m))
  intro h
  have hd : ((m - 1 : ℕ) : ZMod (2 * m)) = 0 := by
    have : ((m : ℕ) : ZMod (2 * m)) - ((1 : ℕ) : ZMod (2 * m)) = 0 := by
      push_cast; linear_combination -h
    rwa [← Nat.cast_sub (by omega)] at this
  rw [ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff] at hd
  have := Nat.le_of_dvd (by omega) hd
  omega

/-
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

Hypothesis (Hypothesizer).
  B1.  The half rotation is fixed-point-free, so it pairs up the 2m vertices
       into m antipodal pairs — the geometric meaning of "compression".
  B2.  In the automorphism *group*, the half rotation has order exactly 2
       (not merely "squares to identity").
  B3.  (necessity) Odd-order graphs can never be cubic, so the index n/2 is
       always integral for the graphs in scope.
  B4.  (surprising) Not every automorphism witnesses κ ≥ 2: the full rotation
       x ↦ x+1 is a perfectly good automorphism but rotates the cycle by 1, not
       by n/2.  Compression demands the *correct* order-2 symmetry.

  * B2: `halfAut_orderOf` via `orderOf_eq_prime` (2 is prime), proving the
    square is the identity and the map is not the identity.
  * B3: `odd_order_not_cubic` is the contrapositive of `cubic_even_order`.
  * B4: `fullRot` is built exactly like `halfAut` (eight `linear_combination`
    adjacency cases); `fullRot_not_half` then shows `1 ≠ m` in `ZMod (2m)` for
    `m ≥ 2` using a `Nat.cast_sub` reduction and `omega`.

Analysis (Analyst).
  * SURVIVED: all four. B2 upgrades the involution fact to a genuine group-order
    statement, matching the conjecture's wording "automorphism of order 2".
  * The key conceptual separation is B4: the *existence* of automorphisms is
    cheap (the whole cyclic group acts); the content of κ ≥ 2 is the existence
    of one of order 2 acting as a half rotation.  This is why the conjecture is
    nontrivial even though cubic edge-transitive graphs are highly symmetric.
  * "TRUE BUT HARD" remains the full classification-level statement; nothing
    here changes that boundary.

Critique / Adversarial review (Critic).
  * Counterexample hunt for B2: could orderOf be 1?  Only if halfAut = 1, ruled
    out by `halfAut_fixedPointFree` at vertex 0.  Could it exceed 2?  No, the
    square is the identity.  Robust.
  * Counterexample for "any automorphism works": EXACTLY `fullRot_not_half`.
    The attempted over-claim ("every automorphism rotates by n/2") is refuted in
    Lean.  Turned into a precise boundary statement.
  * Anti-triviality: none of these are `decide`/`native_decide`; each uses
    `omega`, `linear_combination`, or `orderOf_eq_prime` with real case work.

Synthesis (Principal Investigator).
  The compression factor κ ≥ 2 is precisely: an order-2, fixed-point-free
  automorphism acting as a half rotation of a Hamiltonian cycle.  We isolated

# Computational Evidence — Hamiltonian Compression Factor of Cubic Edge-Transitive Graphs

This note records the small-case evidence that motivated the formal development
in `HamiltonianCompression.lean` and `HamiltonianCompressionBoundary.lean`.

## 1. Small-case calculations (Möbius ladders `ML m`, circulant `{±1, m}`)

`ML m` has `n = 2m` vertices, is `3`-regular, contains the canonical Hamiltonian
cycle `0,1,…,2m-1`, and carries the half rotation `σ : x ↦ x + m`.

| m | n = 2m | graph        | σ = x↦x+m | σ² | σ acts on cycle as | order of σ |
|---|--------|--------------|-----------|----|--------------------|-----------|
| 2 | 4      | K₄           | x↦x+2     | id | rotation by 2 = n/2| 2         |
| 3 | 6      | K₃,₃         | x↦x+3     | id | rotation by 3 = n/2| 2         |
| 4 | 8      | Wagner (M₈)  | x↦x+4     | id | rotation by 4 = n/2| 2         |
| 5 | 10     | M₁₀          | x↦x+5     | id | rotation by 5 = n/2| 2         |
| 6 | 12     | M₁₂          | x↦x+6     | id | rotation by 6 = n/2| 2         |

In every row `σ` is an automorphism (it permutes the connection set
`{+1, -1, +m}` since `+m ↦ +m`), is fixed-point-free, squares to the identity,
and rotates the Hamiltonian cycle by exactly `n/2`.  Hence `κ(ML m) ≥ 2` for all
`m ≥ 1`.  This is exactly `mobiusLadder_twoSymHamCycle`.

Of these, `ML 2 = K₄` and `ML 3 = K₃,₃` are *edge-transitive*; both are
Hamiltonian, and both attain `κ ≥ 2`, confirming the headline conjecture on the
two smallest cubic edge-transitive graphs.

## 2. Parity check (handshaking)

For a cubic graph, `∑_v deg(v) = 3n = 2·(#edges)`, so `3n` is even and therefore
`n` is even.  Checked for the family above (all `n` even).  Formalized as
`cubic_even_order`; contrapositive `odd_order_not_cubic`.  This guarantees the
quantity `n/2` is always an integer for the graphs in scope.

## 3. Counterexample hunt

* **Drop "Hamiltonian".**  The **Petersen graph** is cubic and edge-transitive
  (indeed distance-transitive) on `10` vertices but is **not Hamiltonian**.  So
  it has no Hamiltonian cycle at all and `κ` is undefined — the hypothesis
  "Hamiltonian connected" in the conjecture is load-bearing.  (Not formalized
  here; the non-Hamiltonicity of Petersen is a known hard fact recorded as a
  boundary, see `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`.)

* **"Any automorphism works?"**  No.  The full rotation `x ↦ x + 1` is also an
  automorphism of `ML m`, but for `m ≥ 2` it rotates the cycle by `1 ≠ n/2`.
  Refuted in Lean as `fullRot_not_half`.  Compression needs the *specific*
  order-2 half rotation.

* **"σ could fail to be order 2?"**  Only if `m = 0` (`n = 0`).  Guarded by
  `1 ≤ m`; `halfAut_orderOf` proves order is exactly `2`.

No counterexample to the formalized statements was found.

## 4. OEIS

The vertex counts of Möbius ladders `2m` (`4, 6, 8, 10, 12, …`) are the even
numbers `≥ 4` (A005843 shifted); no nontrivial sequence is conjectured here, so
no OEIS hit is claimed.

## Scope note

The full conjecture (all Hamiltonian cubic edge-transitive graphs up to 10,000
vertices) requires a classification of cubic edge-transitive graphs that is not
available in Mathlib.  The formal results capture the *mechanism* (half-rotation
symmetry of circulant Hamiltonian cycles) and verify it on the two smallest
edge-transitive instances; see the Lab Notes in the Lean files.
